# Introduction

Galton pooled the heights of men and women and found a curve that looked
closer to a single normal curve than he expected. In Problem 1, you will
build mixtures of two normal curves, see when the hidden groups become
visible, and ask how well one new measurement can be assigned to its
group.

Problem 2 picks up from Lecture 25's omitted-variable story and asks the
opposite question: what happens when we add predictors that carry no
signal? You will first add predictors to a regression whose true slopes
you know, then choose predictors for a fixed dataset by how they perform
on held-out rows, and finally test your chosen model once on fresh data.

## Learning goals

In this assignment, you will...

- build a mixture of two normal curves with `dnorm()` and see when the
  pooled curve shows one peak or two;
- use Bayes's rule to find the probability that a new measurement came
  from each group, with equal and unequal group weights;
- calculate the error rates of a classification rule with `pnorm()`;
- see how adding predictors changes the center and the spread of
  estimated slopes, and the error on training rows and on new rows;
- screen candidate predictors by their gains on validation rows over
  many random splits, then test a chosen model once on held-out data.

# Problem 1 — When can we see two groups?

When Pearson proposed adding two normal curves to describe a set of
measurements, Galton told him that he had tried pooling measurements of
adult men and women. The pooled measurements looked closer to a normal
curve than he had expected. Could someone see the two groups in the
pooled curve? And even if the two group curves are given, how well can
you tell where one new measurement came from? Revisit the
excerpt from Galton's letter. [Stigler, p. 333](https://books.google.com/books?id=M7yvkERHIIMC&pg=PA333)

The excerpt leaves the measured trait and the source of the data open.
Galton separately published standing-height percentiles for visitors to
his Anthropometric Laboratory at the 1884 International Health Exhibition.
The first model below uses the reported female and male medians, 63.3 and
67.9 inches, as normal means. The common standard deviation of 2.7 inches
is a rounded approximation based on the two groups' 5th-to-95th
percentile ranges. [Galton's published percentile table, p. 277](https://galton.org/essays/1880-1889/galton-1885-anthro-lab-results.pdf#page=3)

## Working with `dnorm()`

In Lab 09 you used `rnorm(n, mean, sd)` to draw `n` random numbers from
a normal distribution, and a histogram of many draws took on the
familiar bell shape. `dnorm()` describes that same distribution without
drawing anything: `dnorm(x, mean, sd)` gives the value of the normal
density curve at `x`, the smooth curve those histograms approach. Given
a whole vector of values, it returns one density value for each.
So to draw a curve, make a fine grid of values with `seq()`, compute the
density at each one, and connect the points with `plot(..., type = "l")`
(`"l"` for *line*). Here is the normal curve with mean 0 and standard
deviation 1, drawn between −5 and 5:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
z <- seq(-5, 5, by = 0.01)          # 1001 evenly spaced values from -5 to 5
dens <- dnorm(z, mean = 0, sd = 1)  # the density at each value
length(dens)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1001
```


:::
:::


For a single value, `dnorm()` returns a single density value. At $z = 1$:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.2419707
```


:::
:::


That number, about 0.242, is the density at $z = 1$: the point on the
curve directly above $z = 1$, marked with a dot in the plot below. A
density value is not a probability on its own. Multiplying a curve by a
number multiplies every density value: `0.5 * dens` has the same shape,
with every value halved. `lines()` adds a curve to a plot that already
exists.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(z, dens, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "z", ylab = "Density",
     main = "Normal curve, mean 0, SD 1")
points(1, dnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 1), pch = 19)              # the density at z = 1
segments(1, 0, 1, dnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 1), lty = 3)       # from the axis up to it
lines(z, 0.5 * dens, lty = 2)                                # every density value halved
legend("topright", c("dnorm(z)", "0.5 * dnorm(z)"), lty = c(1, 2),
       lwd = c(2, 1), bty = "n")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hw-08_files/figure-html/dnorm-plot-1.png){width=528}
:::
:::


In the models below, each group has its own normal curve. In Part 1a you
will draw each one this way on a grid of heights in inches, multiply it
by its group's weight, and add the two to get the mixture.

## Working with `pnorm()`

A probability comes from **area** under a density curve.
`pnorm(t, mean, sd)` gives the area under the normal curve to the left
of `t`: the probability that a draw from that distribution is below `t`.
Adding `lower.tail = FALSE` gives the area to the right of `t` instead.
The two areas add to 1, because the whole area under a density curve
is 1.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 1)                      # area below z = 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.8413447
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)  # area above z = 1
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.1586553
```


:::
:::


The shaded regions below are the two areas these lines calculate.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hw-08_files/figure-html/pnorm-plot-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


In Part 1c you will use these areas to find how often a classification
rule guesses the wrong group.

## The models

First draw a group label, $G$: $A$ with probability $w_A$, or $B$ with
probability $w_B$, where $w_A + w_B = 1$. These are the **weights** of
the two groups. Then draw a height $X$ from that group's normal
distribution. We use
the same standard deviation and the same midpoint in all three models.
The second and third rows widen the gap in the first row to see what changes.

| Model | Mean of $A$ (inches) | Mean of $B$ (inches) | Common SD (inches) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Exhibition heights | 63.3 | 67.9 | 2.7 |
| Wider gap | 62.225 | 68.975 | 2.7 |
| Widest gap | 60.2 | 71.0 | 2.7 |

Let $f_A(x)$ and $f_B(x)$ be the values of the two normal density curves
at $x$. Use `dnorm(x, mean = ..., sd = ...)` to evaluate a density curve.
The mixture density is the sum of the two weighted curves,

$$
f(x) = w_A f_A(x) + w_B f_B(x).
$$

It describes the measured heights when the group labels are hidden. Use the
supplied parameters throughout.

## Part 1a — Look at the pooled measurements

In this part the two groups are equally common: $w_A = w_B = \tfrac12$,
so the mixture density is $f(x) = \tfrac12 f_A(x) + \tfrac12 f_B(x)$.

1. Before plotting, predict whether the model based on exhibition
   heights will have one peak or two. Calculate the gap between the two
   means in standard deviation units for each model.
2. Plot the pooled density and the two weighted component curves for
   each model. Use the same scales in all three panels. A grid such as
   `seq(50, 82, by = 0.02)` is fine. Use a line type or color to show
   which curve describes the distribution of the unlabeled heights.
   Between which two of your tested gaps does the pooled curve first
   show two peaks?

## Part 1b — Classify a new measurement

Bayes's rule combines two pieces of information: how often a group is
drawn (its weight) and how much density its curve puts near the observed
height. Given a new height $x$, the model gives

$$
\Pr(G=B\mid X=x) = \frac{w_B f_B(x)}{w_A f_A(x) + w_B f_B(x)}.
$$

1. For the exhibition and widest-gap models, calculate this probability
   at $x=65.6$, $66.6$, and $68.6$ inches. Report it in a table and indicate
   which label you would guess if all wrong guesses cost the same. Mark
   ties. Explain which of these heights stays equally ambiguous as the
   means move farther apart.
2. Return to the exhibition model and change the group probabilities to
   $w_A=0.8$ and $w_B=0.2$. Recalculate the probability at $66.6$ inches.
   Compare your guess with the one from the equal-weight model. What
   information did the new weights add?

## Part 1c — How often will the rule get it wrong?

With equal weights and equal standard deviations, guess $A$ below the
midpoint of the means and $B$ above it. Use the original equal weights
for this part. In every model the midpoint is 65.6 inches.

The midpoint is the rule's **boundary**. For a new height $X$, the rule
guesses $A$ if $X < 65.6$ and $B$ if $X > 65.6$. So "guess $B$" means the
same thing as "$X > 65.6$", and "guess $A$" the same as "$X < 65.6$".

The rule makes an **error** when it guesses $B$ for a height that
actually came from group $A$, or guesses $A$ for a height that actually
came from group $B$. Work out each kind of error separately, then
combine them. The function `pnorm(t, mean = ..., sd = ...)` gives the
area below a threshold $t$. Add `lower.tail = FALSE` for the area above
(see *Working with `pnorm()`* above).

1. **Errors on heights from group $A$.** "Given $G = A$" means: suppose
   the new height came from group $A$. Then $X$ is a draw from $A$'s
   normal distribution, with $A$'s mean and the common standard
   deviation. The rule makes an error if $X$ lands **above** the
   boundary, where it guesses $B$:
   $$
   \Pr(\text{guess } B \mid G = A) = \Pr(X > 65.6 \mid G = A).
   $$
   In the exhibition model, for example, this is the probability that a
   draw from a normal distribution with mean 63.3 and SD 2.7 is above
   65.6 inches. Calculate it for the exhibition and widest-gap models.
   Which tail of $A$'s curve is this, and why?
2. **Errors on heights from group $B$.** Calculate
   $$
   \Pr(\text{guess } A \mid G = B) = \Pr(X < 65.6 \mid G = B)
   $$
   for both models. Which tail of $B$'s curve is this? Compare it with
   your answer to 1.
3. **The overall error rate.** For a new draw whose group we do not
   know, the overall error rate is the probability that the rule guesses
   the wrong group. The draw comes from $A$ with probability $w_A$ and
   from $B$ with probability $w_B$, so
   $$
   \text{overall error} = w_A \Pr(\text{guess } B \mid G = A)
     + w_B \Pr(\text{guess } A \mid G = B).
   $$
   Calculate it for both models with $w_A = w_B = \tfrac12$.
4. Write a short paragraph to Galton. Use your plots and error
   rates to explain how two groups can produce one visible peak, and
   why even two visible peaks leave some individual heights ambiguous.
   If the means were also equal, what could a new height tell you
   about the group that produced it?

# Problem 2 — How many predictors can we afford?

In Lecture 25, leaving a relevant predictor out could change the slope
we estimated for another predictor. What happens when we add predictors
that carry no signal? In the first experiment, the true slopes are
known, so you can check how well least squares recovers them. In the
second, you have a fixed dataset and must decide which columns are worth
keeping from their performance on held-out rows.

## Part 2a — Add predictors to a known signal

In this part you simulate many small studies in which you know the
truth. In each study, all 50 predictors, $X_1$ through $X_{50}$, are
drawn independently from a standard normal distribution. The outcome is
$Y = 2X_1 - 1.5X_2 + \varepsilon$, with independent standard normal
noise $\varepsilon$. Thus $X_1$ and $X_2$ have true slopes 2 and $-1.5$.
Treat the other columns as candidates and see what happens when you
give them room in the fit. Each study has 28 **training rows**, used to
fit the models, and 160 **new rows** drawn from the same rule, used only
to check predictions.

::: callout-tip
## Helper functions in this part

One course-written helper, from `homework_08_helpers.R`, simulates a
study. The other two are ordinary R.

| Call | What it does for you |
|---|---|
| `draw_regression_study()` | Simulates one study from the rule above. It takes no arguments. It returns a **list** of two data frames, each with columns `Y` and `X1` through `X50`: `$train` holds the 28 training rows and `$test` the 160 new rows. Every call makes new random draws, so set the seed first to reproduce a study. For example, after `study <- draw_regression_study()`, fit with `data = study$train` and predict with `newdata = study$test` |
| `reformulate(cols, response = "Y")` | Builds a model formula from a vector of column names. `reformulate(c("X1", "X2"), response = "Y")` gives `Y ~ X1 + X2` |
| `mean((y - pred)^2)` | Mean squared error (MSE), defined below: the average squared difference between observed values `y` and predictions `pred` |
:::

Use the first $p$ columns of predictors, so a model of size $p=5$ uses
`X1` through `X5`; `paste0("X", seq_len(p))` makes those names. Here $p$
counts predictors, and `lm()` also fits an intercept.

**Mean squared error.** To measure how far a model's predictions are
from the observed outcomes, square each prediction error and average
them:
$$
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat y_i)^2,
$$
where $y_i$ is the observed outcome in row $i$, $\hat y_i$ is the
model's prediction for that row, and $n$ is the number of rows. In R
this is `mean((y - pred)^2)`. A smaller MSE means predictions closer to
the outcomes. On the training rows, MSE measures how closely the model
fits the data it was fitted to. On the new rows, it measures how well
the model predicts data it has never seen, and that is what we care
about: we want a model with **low MSE on new rows**.

1. Set the seed to 808 and draw one training set. For $p=28$ and $p=50$,
   report the number of coefficients the model would need, `fit$rank`
   (the number of independent columns in the regression), and the number
   of `NA` coefficients. Why can the full list of coefficients fail to
   have a unique least-squares solution even when the training fit is
   nearly exact? From here on, Part 2a uses only models with fewer than
   28 predictors, $p < 28$.
2. Reset the seed to 808 and repeat the experiment 200 times. Each
   repetition draws a fresh study with `draw_regression_study()` and fits
   all six sizes, $p=2,5,8,12,18,24$, on that study's **same 28 training
   rows**, recording the estimated slopes on `X1` and `X2`. After 200
   repetitions you have 200 estimates of each slope at each $p$, one from
   each simulated study. Find the mean of the 200 estimates at each size,
   and use `var()` to find their variance, which measures how much the
   estimate changes from one simulated study to the next. The template
   supplies code for two plots. The first shows, for each $p$, a boxplot
   of the 200 estimates of each slope, with their mean as a blue dot and
   the true slope as a dashed line. The second shows the variance of each
   slope's estimates against $p$. Explain what the boxes, dots, and lines
   show, and whether the center or the spread of the estimates changes
   more as you add predictors.
3. In the same 200 draws, record the MSE on the training rows and on
   the 160 new rows for each fit. (Reset the seed to 808 and repeat the
   loops from question 2; the same seed gives the same 200 studies.) Plot the two mean MSEs against $p$.
   Remember that the goal is a low MSE on the new rows.
   Where does adding predictors make the training fit look better while
   hurting prediction on new rows? Explain how the slope plots help you
   understand this pattern.

## Part 2b — Screen predictors in one split

`data/screening_development.csv` contains one fixed dataset with 40
rows, a response `Y`, and 50 possible predictors `X1` through `X50`.
An unknown subset of the columns carries signal. In every split you will offer
8 of the 50 predictors. You will use the other data file in Part 2c.

Use one random split to see how the scoring works before repeating it.
Start with `set.seed(20261127)` and draw the rows before drawing the
columns so everyone starts with the same split.

- Sample 28 row numbers without replacement for training. The other
  12 rows are your validation rows. Separately, sample 8 predictor
  names, also without replacement.
- Fit an `lm()` with all the offered predictors kept, on the 28
  training rows, and calculate its MSE on the 12 validation rows. Call
  it $\text{MSE}_{\text{kept}}$.
- For each offered predictor, refit on the same training rows with that
  predictor dropped, and calculate the new model's MSE on the same
  validation rows, $\text{MSE}_{\text{dropped}}$. The gain from keeping
  the predictor is $\text{MSE}_{\text{dropped}}-\text{MSE}_{\text{kept}}$.
  Call it a win for that predictor if its gain is positive.

1. Show the gain table for your first split and identify the winners.
   Explain what a positive gain tells you about a predictor **in that
   particular fit and split**.
2. Repeat the whole procedure above 300 times in all, counting your
   first split as one of them. Each time, use the same development
   dataset but draw a new split of the rows and a new set of 8
   predictors, then calculate the gains. Because each split offers only
   8 of the 50 predictors, each predictor is offered in only some of the
   300 splits. For each predictor, count how many splits it was offered
   in, average its gains over those splits, and find the fraction of
   those splits in which it was a win. Show the ten predictors with the
   highest average gain. Why divide the number of wins by the number of
   times that predictor was offered, rather than by 300?

## Part 2c — Choose a model and test it once

1. Use the screening table to choose a final set of predictors. State
   your rule and the names you kept before reading the test file. For
   example, you can look for a clear gap between the strongest average
   gains and the rest, using the win fractions as context.
2. Refit your chosen model on **all 40 development rows**. Now load
   `data/screening_test.csv` and report its root mean squared error
   (RMSE, the square root of MSE) on the 200 fresh rows. Compare it with
   the RMSE from predicting the development mean of `Y` for every test
   row. Explain why the 300 splits, which reuse development rows, play
   a different role from this final test.
